narrative: The model estimated a 61.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt; because that risk was high enough to trigger rejection, your law school application was denied. The strongest factor was your third-year class-rank decile: at 3, it is well below the average of about 5.8 among accepted students, and it pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. Your first-year rank also mattered: a decile of 3, compared with an accepted-student average of 6, added further weight toward failure. By contrast, your LSAT score of 36, slightly below the accepted-student average of 37.2, was the top factor among those three that leaned toward passing rather than failing. In other words, your early and third-year academic standing outweighed the positive signal from your LSAT. To move forward, ask admissions whether the decision can be reconsidered and how to provide context about your academic record. Focus on a concrete plan to strengthen your academic profile, such as retaking relevant coursework or explaining circumstances behind your rank, and ask the law school about bar-readiness support. If you reapply, show improved academic performance and evidence of preparation for bar-level study.
